options: Flips qubit 1 unconditionally
Flips qubit 1 only if qubit 0 is in state |1>
Flips qubit 0 only if qubit 1 is in state |1>
Swaps the states of qubit 0 and qubit 1
questions.explain: cx(control, target) is the controlled-X gate: here qubit 0 is the control and qubit 1 is the target, so qubit 1 is flipped only when qubit 0 is |1>.

questions.q: Why does the order of arguments in qc.cx(a, b) matter?
options: It doesn't matter — cx is symmetric
The first argument is the control and the second is the target, so swapping them changes which qubit conditions the flip of the other
It only matters for circuits with more than 2 qubits
It changes the number of classical bits needed
questions.explain: cx(control, target) is not symmetric: swapping the arguments swaps which qubit acts as the decider and which acts as the follower, producing a different circuit.

questions.q: For the Bell-state circuit qc.h(0); qc.cx(0,1), what are the exact ideal probabilities?
options: P(00)=1.0, all others 0
questions.explain: The Bell state (|00>+|11>)/sqrt(2) has amplitude 0.7071068 on |00> and |11>, giving exact probability 0.5 to each, and exactly zero amplitude (and probability) on |01> and |10>.

questions.q: A real 1024-shot run of the Bell-state circuit gave {'00': 503, '11': 521, '01': 0, '10': 0}. What distinguishes the 503/521 split from the 0/0 outcomes?
options: Both are equally due to statistical shot noise and would change on a rerun
The 503/521 split is shot noise around a true 50/50 probability; the 0s are a structural zero that will remain exactly 0 on every rerun, since those outcomes have zero amplitude
The 0/0 outcomes are shot noise, while 503/521 is a structural property of the circuit
Neither reflects anything about the circuit's true probabilities
questions.explain: 503 vs. 521 is ordinary sampling variation around an exact 50/50 ideal split. In contrast, |01> and |10> have exactly zero amplitude in the Bell state, so they can never occur, on any run, regardless of shot count or seed.

questions.q: What makes entanglement different from ordinary classical correlation between two qubits?
options: Entangled qubits must be physically touching
Entanglement means the joint state cannot be explained by each qubit independently having a definite value before measurement
Entanglement only happens after measurement
Entanglement is identical to classical correlation, just given a different name
questions.explain: In the Bell state, neither qubit has a definite value before measurement, yet measuring one qubit determines the other's outcome with certainty — a correlation with no classical analogue of two independently-determined values.
